subject: Pilot ops questions — latency/concurrency sizing + cost levers
messages:
From: Tom Hayes <tom.hayes@orbithealth.ai>
To: Markus Klein <markus.klein@redwood.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>
Cc: Elena Park <elena.park@orbithealth.ai>
Date: 2026-11-29T14:05:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Quick follow-up from today’s demo — latency & streaming targets

Thanks for the call earlier — quick recap + clarifying questions from our side. We want to make sure the pilot exercise measures the right things so we can sign faster. Key points: 

- Target SLOs we discussed: 95th percentile latency (inference time) for short-turn prompts (<=64 tokens) should be under 200ms end-to-end. For streaming use-cases (longer doc summarization, partial streaming of tokens) we expect partial tokens to arrive within 300ms of prompt acceptance, final generation may be longer.
- Throughput & concurrency: baseline is ~600 QPS for short-turn traffic (peak weekday daytime), ability to sustain bursts up to ~1,500 QPS for short periods (~10 mins). For streaming sessions we expect ~150 concurrent long sessions.
- Workload mix: approximately 70% short queries, 30% long/streaming. Typical short requests return 8–64 tokens; streaming flows can be 1k–2k tokens generated over time.

Questions we need answered before we commit to a Dedicated pilot:
1) Rough sizing: what Dedicated pool footprint would you reserve for the baseline+burst profile?
2) Cost levers: how much can continuous batching, prefix caching, and quantization reduce per-request unit cost in practice? Any example tradeoffs?
3) Caching scope: can caching be cross-user (shared across customers) or must it be per-tenant? How do you handle cache invalidation for prompt variants?
4) Fallbacks: if the preferred model is saturated, what are recommended fallback model variants and quality expectations?

We attached the call recording and a short list of security/retention questions (attached). Please include a short Mutual Action Plan (MAP) and a pilot kickoff checklist in your reply.

Thanks,
Tom Hayes
Head of Product, OrbitHealth

Attachments: orbit-call-recording.mp3 (audio), orbit-security-questions.pdf (PDF)
From: Markus Klein <markus.klein@redwood.com>
To: Tom Hayes <tom.hayes@orbithealth.ai>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-11-29T16:12:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Quick follow-up from today’s demo — latency & streaming targets

Tom — thanks for the clear recap. Below is a compact response to each ask plus proposed next steps for a 2-week Dedicated pilot so you can validate both latency and cost tradeoffs.

1) Sizing (initial recommendation):
- Baseline pool: 8 x A100-equivalent GPU workers (mixed optimized instances) to cover 600 QPS for short-turns with a comfortable headroom for concurrency and streaming.
- Burst buffer: autoscale policy to add up to +6 workers (total 14) for short-lived peaks; use queue-based throttling for graceful degradation.

2) Cost/perf levers (summary):
- Continuous batching: groups short-turns into micro-batches (~40–80ms window). Improves GPU utilization and reduces per-token cost by ~20–40% depending on prompt length distribution. Adds tail variance: p95 delta typically +10–30ms on short-turns with aggressive batching windows.
- Prefix/KV caching: sticky-prefix and KV cache reduce repeated token recomputation for repeated contexts (chat histories, shared prompts). Effective if you have high reuse; can cut token compute by 15–50% by workload.
- Quantization profiles: int8 or 4-bit quantization can lower inference latency and memory pressure; expect ~25–40% cost reduction at some quality risk for sensitive generation tasks (we'll profile your prompts).
- Model variants: recommend a primary medium-latency variant (redwood-medium-8q) for most requests and a high-capacity fallback (redwood-large-4q) for complex streaming or long-context requests. Fallback routing can be region-aware.

3) Caching scope & invalidation:
- We support tenant-scoped caches by default. Cross-tenant shared caches are possible but require strict prompt-normalization and security review; not common for PHI use-cases. Invalidation is policy-driven (time-to-live, explicit purge on model updates).

4) Pilot plan & MAP:
- Deliverables we propose: pilot capacity sheet (attached), a 2-week traffic replay + synthetic ramp, SLA targets for p50/p95/p99 for short-turns and streaming partials, and a short MAP with success criteria (latency p95 <200ms for short-turns, streaming partial latency <300ms 95% of the time, and cost per short-turn under agreed budget).

Next steps:
- I’ll share the pilot-capacity-sheet.xlsx and a one-page MAP. Can we lock a kickoff on Tuesday (2026-12-01) at 9:30am PT? Karthik will be the SE on the engagement and Marissa will oversee delivery from Redwoods side.

Attaching: pilot-capacity-sheet.xlsx, mutual-action-plan.docx

Cheers,
Markus Klein
Head of Sales, Redwood Inference

Attachments: pilot-capacity-sheet.xlsx (spreadsheet), mutual-action-plan.docx (doc)

Subject: Re: Quick follow-up from today’s demo — latency & streaming targets

Thanks Markus — that all makes sense. A few clarifications from our product side: 

- Usage mix confirmation: 70/30 short vs long matches our instrumentation. Short requests are small but have tight p95 SLAs and are latency-sensitive for the clinician UX.
- Caching: cross-tenant caching is a no-go due to PHI. Tenant-scoped caching is fine — please note we will need encryption at rest and strict TTLs.
- Quantization: we’re open to profiling int8 but need a sample-run with our prompts to validate no accuracy regressions on entity extraction.

Can you include a rough cost-range for the 2-week pilot (estimate both hosted and Dedicated options) and an expected timeslot for the Tuesday kickoff? Also attaching our security questionnaire — SOC2 and retention answers will be required for procurement.

Tom

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.com>

Cc: Markus Klein <markus.klein@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-11-30T13:07:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Quick follow-up from today’s demo — latency & streaming targets

Tom — thanks, quick sizing + cost sketches below (initial, ballpark figures to move the MAP forward). Happy to refine once we profile your prompt set.

Pilot sizing options (2-week):
- Dedicated small (cost-conscious): 6 GPUs, conservative autoscale to +3. Good for validating correctness under limited throughput. Estimated pilot compute cost (2 weeks, incl infra & support): ~$18k–$25k.
- Dedicated recommended (production-like): 12 GPUs with burst to 18 via autoscale. Estimated pilot compute cost: ~$34k–$48k.
- Hosted quick test: use Redwood Hosted with fixed concurrency lanes and autoscaling; cheaper to start but won't mirror dedicated networking/isolated performance. Estimated hosted test: ~$6k–$9k.

Cost levers & expected impact (practical notes):
- Continuous batching window: 20–50ms window gives most of the utilization gains with ~10–15ms added tail for p95 in many cases. Larger windows (80–120ms) reduce cost more but push p95 higher — not recommended for the clinician UX.
- Prefix/KV cache: for tenant-scoped caches, expect material savings if you have repeated conversations or templates. Cache efficiency depends on normalization; we’ll provide a short instrumentation script.
- Quantization: profiling required — on average int8 gives ~30% token compute reduction. For entity-aware prompts we will compare F1 scores on your evals; if drop >2–3% we recommend fallback to higher-precision variant for those prompts.

Fallback model strategy: route to redwood-medium-8q as primary; if queue depth > threshold or p95 exceeds target route to redwood-small-16q for strict latency-sensitive short-turns (lower quality but faster) or to redwood-large-4q for streaming/long-context reliability. We’ll include rollback policies.

Security & retention notes: we support per-tenant encryption at rest, VPC peering for Dedicated, and can align on retention TTLs for call transcripts/logs. I’ll answer the SOC2 fields in the questionnaire and return it with signatures.

Regards,
Karthik Iyer
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
